title: ⭐⭐ Revision: from the leaflet to the poem

questions.prompt: A guide stops in the courtyard: "This is a two-hundred-year-old fig tree." Unpack the compound — which sentence says exactly the same thing?

options.text: The fig tree is two hundred years old.
The fig tree has two hundred years.
The fig tree is two-hundred-year-old.
The fig tree is aged of two hundred years.

questions.explanation: Once the compound leaves its place in front of the noun, it has to be unpacked, and English unpacks an age with the verb be: the tree is two hundred years old. Saying that it "has" two hundred years copies French straight into English and is the most frequent age mistake of the bac. Leaving the compound whole after be is the other half of the mistake — a compound of measurement only works in front of its noun. And "aged of" is a translation too: we write aged two hundred, with no of.

questions.prompt: English puts the main stress on the FIRST word of a compound noun — a FILM director, a BOX office — while an ordinary adjective and its noun keep it on the noun. In which of these phrases does the main stress fall on the first word?

options.text: an empty gallery
a live band
a long interval
a concert hall

questions.explanation: A concert hall is one thing with one name, a compound noun in two words, so the stress moves forward onto CONcert — the same movement as in FILM director and BOX office. The three others are an adjective describing a noun, and there the noun keeps the stress: an empty GALLery, a live BAND, a long INterval. The difference is audible and it carries meaning: a BLACKbird is a species, a black BIRD is any bird of that colour.

questions.prompt: A theatre programme prints two compounds one line apart: "an actor-training director" and "an actor-trained director". The two endings send the arrow in opposite directions. Which pair of readings is right?

options.text: actor-training = the director was trained by actors; actor-trained = he trains them
actor-training = the director trains actors; actor-trained = he was trained by them
both compounds say the director trains actors, since the endings do the same job
both compounds say the director was trained by actors, whichever ending is printed

questions.explanation: The -ing form makes the noun in front of it the receiver of the action, so an actor-training director trains actors, exactly as an elephant-training centre trains elephants. The past participle makes that same noun the doer, so an actor-trained director is one whom actors trained — the way a hand-painted poster was painted by hand. Ask yourself who does the action before you read the ending, because reading both compounds the same way throws the whole distinction away.

questions.prompt: A festival poster announces a "posthumous album" by a singer. What does the word tell you?

options.text: it was recorded before he was famous
it came out after his death
it brings together his greatest hits
it was released without his agreement

questions.explanation: Posthumous describes anything that happens after a person has died — a posthumous album, a posthumous prize, posthumous fame. It says when, not how: the songs may be old recordings or new mixes, and the singer's family may well have agreed to the release. Nor does the word promise a collection of hits; that is what a compilation is. Keep it beside the other words of praise from the same page: pioneering, single-handedly, stature and indisputably.

questions.prompt: Read this pair aloud: "They will record the concert." · "The record sold a million copies." Where does the main stress fall in each?

options.text: RE-cord in the first sentence, re-CORD in the second
RE-cord in the first, and RE-cord in the second too
re-CORD in the first, and re-CORD in the second too
re-CORD in the first sentence, RE-cord in the second

questions.explanation: Some two-syllable words are a noun and a verb at once, and English keeps them apart with the stress alone: the verb takes it on the second syllable, the noun on the first. To re-CORD the concert is the action, so the first sentence moves it forward; a RE-cord that sold a million copies is the object, so the second pulls it back — the same movement as to pre-SENT a prize and a PRE-sent under the tree. Nothing in the spelling tells you which one you are reading: the sentence does, and your voice has to show it.

questions.prompt: The cinema prints its prices: "Adults £8.50 · Children aged 3 to 14 £5.25 · Under 3 free". Sami is 14 and brings his sister, who is two. What do the two of them pay altogether?
questions.explanation: Place each visitor in a category before you add anything. "Aged 3 to 14" includes fourteen, so Sami pays the child price of £5.25; his sister is two, which falls under three, so she pays nothing — and £5.25 plus nothing is £5.25. Paying twice the child price forgets that free means free, £13.75 promotes Sami to the adult rate he has not reached, and £8.50 charges an adult who is not there. In a price list the boundary words — under, aged, up to, from — do as much work as the figures.
